newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Callback systems eat into Brazil phone revenues.
newsitem.headline: Callback systems eat into Brazil phone revenues.

text.p: The growing popularity of callback systems to escape Brazil's sky-high telephone rates costs state long-distance operator Embratel eight percent of its annual international call revenue, an official said.
"We are losing today the equivalent of eight percent of net international receipts to the callback system," said an Embratel spokesman, who asked not to be named.
He could not provide a figure for the losses or Embratel revenues so far this year.
The source denied newspaper reports which quoted Embratel chief Dilio Penedo as saying callback-related losses totalled 23 million reais last year.
But he admitted that commercial users today are increasingly resorting to callback systems offered by a variety of foreign firms to avoid Brazil's notoriously high long-distance tariffs.

According to telecoms experts, the callback market worldwide is growing at an annual rate of between 20 percent and 25 percent and some 300 firms offer the service around the globe, including more than two dozen serving Latin America.

Lydia Rodriguez, an AT&T spokeswoman, said the U.S. telecoms giant is projecting "double-digit" growth in the callback market for Latin America but said company officials declined to provide more details on the market projections.
"It's a very active market and will continue to grow in the region until rates become more competitive," she added.
Under the callback method, a caller rings up a computer overseas, hangs up and then waits for the computer to call back with an open line -- and a cheaper rate.
Savings can be substantial. Using the system, a call to Japan costs 1.15 reais a minute compared to 3.39 reais with Embratel.
Embratel, a unit of the federally owned Telebras long-distance and satellite services.
In 1995, it posted a net profit of 137.96 million reais and gross operating receipts of 1.4 billion reais.
International calls last year accounted for 20 percent of net receipts of 30 million reais.
The spokesman said he did not know the percentage lost last year to callback systems but said it was "much lower" than the present eight-percent rate.
Embratel officials contend Brazil's rates are high partly because of an 18.55 percent tax on international calls, compared with seven or eight percent in other countries.
Embratel's goal is to reduce taxes on those calls to around 10 percent "to make them internationally competitive."
Brazilian legislation does not bar the use of callback systems but officials consider it "fiscal evasion," the spokesman said.
"It's an evasion of taxes," he said.
He added many foreign firms, including major operators, offer callback services to Brazil. But he declined to name any for fear of upsetting those with whom Embratel has trade accords.
"You must understand, Embratel has commercial agreements with 350 firms around the world," he said.
-- Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 232 4411
